He'd played with a ball on his parents' office carpet that made harmonious popping sounds when he bounced it. Then he sat by the grandfather clock while he played. His favorite song had ten notes, each one a different color, and sometimes when he was sick at night and his mother played it for him it made everything okay.

These days the music lived in his brain. His favorite songs were the ones that started with several seconds of silence, because sometimes his friends would be talking about dumb stuff and if he sat in just the right position he could hear the music. He closed his eyes and looked for a note, a yellow one, and when he found it he began to play.

In P.E., Dylan's gym teacher asked him to play "Let It Snow" for the class, which had a hundred people in a circle around him. But he was so nervous he couldn't remember how the song started, and by the time he found a note it was all wrong. Some of the kids laughed and some of them frowned and then the teacher told him to stop. Later in the day his mom said Principal Teverbaugh wanted to talk to him in his office.

Dylan was nervous because he hadn't gotten called in before, but once he got there he thought of a cool song he could play. In the magic show he'd seen last summer, the magician had turned cards into floating flowers. So Dylan imagined the papers on the principal's desk turning into things he liked. A pencil turning into a giant blue-green frog, a stapler turning into a six-foot gorilla that walked outside and into the woods never to return. Principal Teverbaugh didn't notice, but he did ask Dylan to play "Let It Snow."

"I can't," Dylan said. "It's too hard. I'm not ready for it."

Behind the house the river curved sharply into a hillside. When it first showed up on the map, it wasn't noticeable from the air. It was about fifteen feet deep, too shallow to show up clearly on sonar. No rocks or trees or logs sat near the banks; the white mister of the falls was invisible. The river didn't drain farmland; it just sat in a ring of woods. The engineers typically saw these systems as holes in the landscape, like a data pixel in a spreadsheet marked N/A.

This one was different. A two-person raft team on the river found the waterfall, and textbook erosion patterns on the rock near the banks. Photos on the Internet paired the landscape with an unreleased nature documentary called Amazon Vale, which no one had heard of. The team sent the data back to Rio. Rio sent the Scouts, who now assembled in secret by the ruined Agua Boa bridge. Tiago had spent his whole life preparing for this moment.

First the Scouts would pan the trees below the falls, watching for animal movement as they fell, looking for familiar patterns through the mists. If they saw a mammal on camera, they would return with the larger Scouts and mark it with an air gun. They would hunt for nests and settle in below them to wait for babies, or take adult birds on the ground. Ground teeth and vampire bats preferred the canopy, nesting close to one another by the roads ahead. Their bulky young took almost a year to adapt to drinking blood, longer still to learn how to fly. Regardless, the Scouts would cauterize any wounds they weren't able to kill. As they bowed down and prayed, the wounded animals would be their reward.

Then came animal bots, cameras and earplugs and tracking devices set to record the bustle of bird songs and lizard chirps, strung in lines between trees and shining with solar glitter. Switching On: An interview with FRICTION's co-editor Aleksandar Hemon

By Fay Stevens

Editorial Assistant, fRICTION Magazine

Prior to joining the staff at FRICTION, Aleksandar Hemon was something of a literary polyglot. A literary translator working primarily with Serbo-Croatian (as well as French, Hungarian, and Telugu), Hemon has authored, co-authored or co-edited 16 books, the bulk of which are translations of other writers' works.

Born in Sarajevo, Hemon left Bosnia in 1992 with his family before the brutal and unnecessary destruction of the city at the hands of the Army of the Republic of Serb in a multi-day shootout which liquified human bodies and strained faucets of drinking water down the street. Hemon, his wife, and four children (who managed to hide in a shed) endured sixteen shells which totally destroyed his home. It was twelve years later, when he reached adulthood, that Hemon finally wrote about the experience, giving us one of FRICTION's nagging, inimitable chroniclers in an essay titled "The Accordionist's Son."

Hemon came to America and enrolled himself in the graduate program at Northwestern University – where he would meet Nicole Krauss and David Bezmozgis, two of Hemon's now extremely successful friends and co-workers. In 1996, he published "Nowhere Man," an essay manuscript which went on to win the 1998 New York Public Library Young Lions Fiction Award. Hemon

Jen's Sprint started reluctantly. She had old snow tires, but the tires on the Prius and on her dad's minivan looked brand new. She'd had meetings all day, and sat on the phone with a state rep for two hours until he told her, in a private moment of exasperation, that the better question was why there were so many male legislators who felt comfortable admitting that they couldn't speak to women in polite company, let alone in chambers. Jen saw the text as she pulled out of the driveway. Halfway to school she noticed a Turn Around sign in front of the car in front. There was a single-track roadblock on the beach ridge—the line of hills across the city where the school sat. Beyond that she would have to re-trace her route to get Theo. It could take her an hour.

A school bus pulled up behind her, not the kind that stopped for her son, too big, but some kind of specialized equipment bus. It stopped and the driver got out and walked around back. Behind new headlights the bus opened. From it stepped a person that Jen only then realized was Theo, his knees rubbery, his hair mussed, and his small face twisted into what might have been disbelief or grief.

Theo had to have spent five minutes thinking through the excuse that he could give that would serve two purposes, one to explain why he hadn't been picked up yet, and two to tell him that the concert would be cancelled. He would have put his belongings silently in the bus, sat down in the seat and thought about telling Jen, until finally the idea simply became unbearable.

We all have blind spots—we have tunnel vision at least once in our life—where we lose sight of the person next to us, and we do not know.

Before the gym was full of kids, a bell rang and Theo's homeroom teacher took them to the gym stage, the rest of the school humming in the halls behind them. One student took first place on the stage and sang a song, then another, the teachers smiling from the front row. When it was Theo's turn, he took the microphone and sang.

Later, he made it through the picture line quickly with Jen, wearing his white and gold winter concert T-shirt, just clear of the snowflakes in the air. The crowd at picture time held the air before them as still as they could, all eyes on their children, asking Jen, "Does he stutter?" Jen shook her head. "My older son doesn't either. It's lucky you fixed that." Jen put on a smile.

Without breaking the lines, Jen helped Theo put ice skates on for the skating rink after the concert. A bouncy castle across the gym floor moved in the air instead of on the ground in the five feet of snow still falling. Jen's phone died as she took a picture of Theo skating, so she texted her parents that he'd sung, and wasn't stuttering at all. Then she dropped her own phone in the snow.

Later, Jen's parents would call to tell her that they didn't see any sense in leaving Duluth at the last minute, and they had waited until the snow slowed down before driving to visit their other grandson, who'd gotten a minor concussion playing football.

A coordinated stomp of snow boots walked past Jen and Theo, and the skating rink was mostly empty. They went to weigh themselves, Jen's parents having bought Theo a cake for losing weight over winter break. When they stepped off the scale, the cake was too heavy to fit in his backpack, so they tied it to the handle. Jen shoved her gloved hand deeper into her pocket to feel for her hotel key card, but it was missing, so she snuck a peek to make sure it was still there.

To Jen it was unthinkable. Her phone filled up with text messages from parents, friends, other mothers, all of them asking how Theo was taking it. It was praise — "That little guy is so brave" — and advice to take him to Dairy Queen to buy ice cream to get his mind off it, and suggestions that he could give a private performance in the school library so that everyone who'd driven from two hundred miles away could see his solo without having to go home.

Jen stood in the cow pasture behind their house, out of sight of the house and cars in the street. She watched the ground swell with flakes. The wind made patterns on the snow, dimples and furrows. "Gonna get nippy," Theo said and she started to turn around to go in and stop yelling at herself for being so stupid when she heard a voice behind her. The herd of cows was coming back from the cornfield. She'd fed them before the school bus that morning.

Almost every elementary in Jen's district had had a concert, although it was January already and the middle and high school concerts had passed weeks ago. That was one reason Jen had puzzled over the cancellation notice: her school had, just like every other, cancelled kindergarten orientation and all concerts in October, in November, and once in December. But there had always been another concert, even when the forecast changed hours before it started. She had been worried about cancellation since the forecast that afternoon, but six inches was a lot of snow. And there must not be other rooms available because the cancellation notice didn't suggest that they could postpone to later that evening or the next day.

So Jen took little Mia from daycare after work and waited for the call that would tell her to bring her coats up to school. It didn't come. Jen ate dinner. Mia ate dinner, too. Jen fell asleep on the sofa and Mia fell asleep in my arms.

A snow plow hid a half-inch of snow in knots. I woke and carried Mia to bed and locked the door behind me.

At 6:30 the phone rang. Theo, crying. "Mom," he said, "the concert's been cancelled!" Jen called the school office. They said call the concert director.

"At Hawthorne, every student has a job," said the director. "Someone's got to be the emcee and someone's got to introduce every solo act. There are forty kids with jobs, and it simply will not work if only some of them come."

"Understood," Jen said. "What if there's a county-wide black-out and the phones stop working?"

"Good point," the director said. "Everyone needs to come."

Jen hung up. "Theo!" she said. "There's another concert!"

Theo leaped out of bed, washed his face, and pulled on his boots. Jen shrugged on her parka, waked Mia out of her dreams and into her pajamas. They all hopped in the car, cheered when it started, cheered again when they reached the main street. The snow had stopped in the afternoon. At 8 p.m. the snow was coming down so hard sounds from the outside world got muffled. Jen couldn't hear her phone buzz with the message "weather do it!" She texted her sister to check the weather. The wind blew hard enough her friend's porch sign fell off.

She didn't check the weather until an hour later, when the ground was covered in snow and the roads hadn't been plowed. Her phone was dead. She missed the texts:  "I'm not afraid of the weather" and "Cold weather, hot concert, amIRite?" 'Okay, fine," she texted. "See you soon."

Jen was six, Theo was two, when they fell through the ice at Flatley lake and he forgot how to talk. He couldn't speak at all for a week, and it took a month before he started to put sentences together. When he stuttered, his emotions were big and his breathing forced. He kept to himself. It was like his eyes turned inward, and he didn't want to talk to anyone.

With a bad speech block he began to second-guess himself. He stopped raising his hand, stopped talking to his teachers, mumbled when they asked him questions. At a checkup, speech-language pathologist said he had 'disfluency,' which helped him understand what was happening when he tried to talk.

The pathologist showed him games that showed what it was like to walk or swim with shoes or wading boots on. He understood right away -- they were too heavy. She showed him fun breathing games with bubbles and yarn that loosened up the weight in his voice.

World around us slideshow »

As his speech got better, he got bolder. But by eighth grade the stutter started to creep back, and it started to follow him into places he didn't want it to go. One day he wrote a poem for his creative writing class. He practiced speaking its first line a dozen times in the hallway outside the classroom, over and over, slower and louder each time. The teacher told him to recite it in front of the class, and he couldn't reply.

A few days later, the stutter was in the lunchroom. He couldn't order his food. He waved for an aide to handle it. After class, the stutter didn't leave him. It didn't matter whether he was alone in the hallway or not, he talked to himself whenever no one else was around.

The thing I remember most is not being able to imagine marrying some nice, Loyal Church-Going Lutheran minister. I can remember my roommate in college explaining she wanted to go to seminary. I understood the whole wanting to help people thing, but I'm pretty sure I was thinking, Good for you? That is your brand of crazy?

After college I thought I wanted to teach kids, but the evening when I was thinking that my mom was telling me that the government was going to pass a law saying public school teachers could only teach divinity so I should go work at a Christian school. I was seventeen and we were sitting in a room at a BBQ at Hillary and Matt's house doing our sweetie pie, lovin' fleet pillow talk and my mom tried to tell me this. I can remember thinking to myself, if that happens I will be very, very upset and will likely lash out at my husband in bed in a single, brutal motion. It also occurred to me that if I got married to Loyal Church-Going Lutheran Minister man at some point I would become a nice, not very interesting person who buys my wardrobe at the JC Penney's outlet.

I was an Romeo-and-Juliet-over-the-wall type of love when it came to a husband. I knew it would be a man who would look at me with eyes full of earnest desire, not knowing what the next person would say or do so he would listen. Not knowing what to say but wanting with his whole spirit and being to listen. I just knew. I just knew that is what I wanted.

It was years later, when I was reconciled to lifting a course like Feminist Theology as a married woman in a grocery store in a bad mood, (it happens sometimes, I might say) that I decided I didn't have to be a pastor's wife ever. I didn't have to have children, give up work, or unlearn a lifelong cheer. That was my moment of freedom to be motivated to deep, heady, intellectual conversation with deep thinkers and great books. To be myself. It was freeing.

"Just breathe," she whispered against his hair.

His music teacher nodded and faced the kids, the parents, the sea of hats and mittens. She calmed her nerves. "Our first performer has something very special planned. So, ready? Theo Kowal."

Theo stood up and held the microphone by the stand. His teacher patted his elbow and stepped back. He closed his eyes. He could feel the breath in his lungs, and the way his throat vibrated when his breath came out, and the tik-tik-tik of his heartbeat—it came sometimes, late at night, sharper and faster than this.

He opened his eyes, and the first note shimmered out. His voice straightened itself into the silence of the gym and didn't shake all the way through. The words came easy, one by one, softly at first, and more sure as he went on—

I've rarely seen a 
white Christmas...

The hundredth year of public schools in that town, Jen thought. Egyptian potatoes and Shakespeare and calculus and the county bus driver and half a dozen fights at lunch, snowflake by snowflake, year by year. All of it in Theo's voice, clear and strong and unafraid. 

By the time he'd sung the last note, the room was very quiet.

Theo sat back down. He heard his teacher say "Thank you" but couldn't see her. Someone was clapping. Then ten people. Then nearly everyone. Jen clapped until her hands hurt. By the time Theo looked up, everyone was on their feet.

As the snow thickened around them, she put her arms around him and pressed a kiss into the top of his head. His cheeks were red from the cold and something else, and his eyelashes were wet.

"Now you know," she said.

"I know," he said.

The muscles in his jaw loosened and his arms settled at his sides. He hit the high note and held it steady, and everyone in the auditorium was silent but for him.

There was fresh snow on the roads that night. Jen walked to the parking lot underneath a sky of swirling flakes and steady wind. Her parents were already there, waiting by the car, and when Theo came out of the door he ran the last hundred feet without hesitation.

He said, "What about the ski conditions?"

"That's only for real snow, anyway," she said. "So I have to get used to singing alone in front of the whole school. And not stutter."

Jen wanted to hug his head to her chest and hold it there until he was twenty-three. She said, "Can I ask what all this is for?"

"The math teacher once said that singing in front of the class over and over makes it go away. For me."

"Was the math teacher right?" Her heart beat against the steering wheel.

"I don't think so."

They talked about packing the powder in the tips, which way the wind would come off the Edges, and waved to Mrs. Spellington and Mrs. Dillinger as they walked down the downtown sidewalk from the big window at Borders. They settled in at the screened-in porch at Springbrook with a carafe of coffee for Jen, mountain dew for Theo, and spicy raisins to encourage the whole thing along. Theo ordered the Ishi.

By dinnertime Jen felt trimmed, sharp, with something cool and not hesitant sitting behind her eyes. She even found herself sewing again, just playing with the machine before their pajama party shift was supposed to start in a few hours. Theo leaned against the counter and watched.

He didn't turn away, didn't look at the floor and avoid her bruises as he had for years. Instead he asked her what she'd drawn on the back of the fabric. Squares, circles, arrows, dashes, and an elephant trying to get out. He said, "What's this?"

She tucked the needle under her finger and closed the grinder. "You've never asked before."

"I don't know. I just never did, I guess."

"Surprise!" Mrs. Mansfield said. Out back where no one could see came several neighborhood families with the sound system and lights from the office. The driveway filled with cars. Someone brought hot cider.

Afterward, inside, Theo held out his father's borrowed guitar. "There's someone here who wants to show you something," Mrs. Mansfield said. At first, looking at everyone, his face turned red. Then he began, "Let it snow, let it snow, let it..." A little too fast, but his voice never wavered, not once. He talked later about the day he'd stood on the stage and played " 'Let It Snow' by itself." And when Mrs. Mansfield said thank you so much, the kids clapped, and Jen knew why she had stayed here, in tiny, windy White Earth, when this was how the townspeople lived.

She'd escorted Jen's parents to their car, but her father was running back and kissing her both cheeks when he saw Jen in the doorway. "Something's happened," he said. "I just saw that sign in the window."

"Which sign?" said Jen.

"The concert's canceled!" Jen said. Her father looked in the gifted-services window. "Oh," he said. "Oh dear." Jen handed her mother a mug of coffee. "We can pick up something for dinner," she said, and her mother smiled. Maybe they'd watch a movie at home.

Theo's teachers made him put his concert shirt back on and walk with the other kids to the gyms of the junior highs where other elementary schools' concerts had been canceled. Jen, his parents, and her husband followed. When they arrived, the kids were all lined up in school colors on the stage and showing the parents where to find their family. Theo waved to Jen's father and they waved back. Theo's position halfway up the hall made it hard to see. Jen was on his left, just out of his field of view, but she felt his disappointment.

The principal, Mr. Frank, came out to the stage: "I am so sorry. We all wanted to see what you all have to offer, but with the weather in the forecast, we had to—" None of the parents could stand to listen. "Just wait until they can get music to these kids," her father said angrily to some nearby parents. Her parents left just as the kids struck up. Her husband, who'd driven to work that day because he had to tend the restaurant, had to get back.

Jen stood with Jen's mother in the dark aisle on Jen's right. Jen usually noticed the new kids who'd lined up wrong, and new teachers teaching music classes for the first time, but she couldn't even see the stage. But every once in a while she saw Theo's face, long and narrow overhis right shoulder: mouth about to open, eyes wide, smiling, but panicked. Jen spun around and held Jen's mother, and Jen's mother held her while the light in Theo's eyes faded.

If anyone noticed that Theo wasn't singing, as he stood there quiet for seven minutes, her family didn't.
